analysis.reason: This is a low-latency BNS early-warning search method for third-generation detectors, useful for compact-object multi-messenger follow-up, but it does not directly study FRB/PRS, supernova engines, jets, neutrinos, or circumstellar interaction.
analysis.result: A CNN with $\mathcal{N}=10^{3}$ templates reaches a sensitivity distance comparable to SFT matched filtering, which instead needs approximately $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=10^{7}$ templates, about four orders of magnitude more. For $f_{\max}=10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $f_{\min}\in\{2,3,4,5\}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, the quoted evaluation time falls from minutes to milliseconds, a speed-up of about $1.6\times10^{4}$–$4.0\times10^{4}$; the CNN per-template cost is $\langle\mathfrak{c}_1\rangle\approx(3$–$25)\,\mu\mathrm{s}$. At fixed template number, sensitivity follows $\langle s\rangle\sim\rho_{\rm opt}^{2}(1-\langle\mu\rangle)$ with $\rho_{\rm opt}^{2}\propto\int_{f_{\min}}^{10\,\mathrm{Hz}}f^{-7/3}/S_n(f)\,df$.
analysis.problem: Early warning of binary neutron-star inspirals in third-generation detectors is limited by the computing cost of evaluating the detection statistic at low latency.
analysis.method: Early inspirals are represented by narrowband SFTs with $T_{\mathrm{SFT}}=31\,\mathrm{s}$ and $\Delta k=51$ bins about $f(t;\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}})=f_{\max}[1+(256/5)(\pi f_{\max})^{8/3}(G\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}}/c^{3})^{5/3}(t_{\max}-t)]^{-3/8}$. A CNN minimizes binary cross-entropy and searches only $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}}$, while the SFT statistic $\mathcal{X}$ is maximized analytically over phase and luminosity distance and then over an eight-dimensional bank. Latency is modeled as $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{N}\langle\mathfrak{c}_1\rangle$, with $f_s=40\,\mathrm{Hz}$ for the 3, 4, and 5 Hz regimes.
limits: For lower chirp masses, evolution from $f_{\min}$ to $f_{\max}$ can exceed the fixed analysis window, so the signal is aligned at $f_{\max}$ and only its late portion is retained.

analysis.reason: This ZTF spectroscopic census of hydrogen-rich SLSNe directly constrains circumstellar interaction, pre-explosion mass loss, and possible Ia-CSM contamination, which are central to supernova-engine and CSM studies.
analysis.result: Of 106 hydrogen-rich SLSNe, 105 show narrow Balmer emission and are spectroscopically SLSNe-IIn; SN 2022lvm is the sole broad-lined SLSN-II in the discussed 2021–2022 subset comparison (1/36, 2.8%). Measured $L_{\mathrm{H}\alpha}$ spans $2.2\times10^{40}$ to $1.5\times10^{42}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ (median $2.6\times10^{41}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$). The median Balmer decrement rises from 2.85 before $+100$ d to 4.40 afterward, below the Ia-CSM comparison medians 6.58 and 17.76. After excluding the SLSN-II and six Ia-CSM-like objects, median shell speed correlates with peak magnitude ($r=0.63$, $p=0.010$): brighter events tend to have lower $v_{\rm s}$. For 13 calibrated objects at $v_{\rm CSM}=100\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ and $\epsilon=0.5$, $\dot{M}\sim0.028$–$0.30\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ from $L=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\dot{M}v_{\rm s}^{3}/u_{\rm w}$. Six of 105 narrow-line events ($\sim6\%$) are Ia-CSM-like. Narrow interaction lines can persist beyond $+200$ d, with no Balmer morphology unique to SLSNe-IIn relative to fainter SNe IIn.
analysis.problem: Whether luminous narrow-line SLSNe-IIn are spectroscopically only the bright extreme of SNe IIn, what dense hydrogen-rich CSM and enhanced pre-explosion mass loss they require, and whether narrow Balmer lines plus high luminosity uniquely imply core collapse rather than Ia-CSM.
analysis.method: The study uses 304 optical spectra of 106 ZTF events selected at rest-frame peak $M\leq-19.9$ mag, with phases $(t-t_{\rm peak})/(1+z)$ and fluxes scaled by $10^{-0.4(m_{\rm GP}-m_{\rm syn})}$ from Gaussian-process light curves (287 absolutely calibrated). Balmer luminosity, pEW and FWHM are measured after local continuum subtraction. Single-epoch Monte Carlo electron-scattering snapshots (escatter; $10^{5}$ H$\alpha$ photons outside a cold dense shell) fit line profiles. Mass-loss rates use $L=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\dot{M}\frac{v_{\rm s}^{3}}{u_{\rm w}}$ and $\dot{M}=\frac{2L}{\epsilon}\frac{u_{\rm w}}{v_{\rm s}^{3}}$, with luminosity integrated from the spectra and a blackbody extension to 3000–20000 Å.
assumptions: Quoted mass-loss rates use the adopted CSM-interaction model with $\epsilon=0.5$ and $v_{\rm CSM}=100\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, commonly with a shock speed of $5000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.
limits: Inferred mass-loss rates are order-of-magnitude estimates rather than precise progenitor mass-loss histories.

analysis.research_progress: The sample shows that SLSN-IIn H$\alpha$ pEW and FWHM overlap those of lower-luminosity SNe IIn, while lines persisting for tens to hundreds of days and $\dot{M}\sim0.028$–$0.30\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ exceed ordinary OB or red-supergiant winds under $L=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\dot{M}v_{\rm s}^{3}/u_{\rm w}$. Brighter events tend toward lower $v_{\rm s}$, consistent with denser or more massive CSM and higher radiative efficiency, and $\sim6\%$ of the narrow-line objects are Ia-CSM-like.

analysis.reason: The paper quantifies radioactive-decay-powered nebular emission, progenitor-mass diagnostics, and internal dust in SN 1987A at 200–800 d, which is useful for separating engine yields and dust from circumstellar interaction, but it does not model the interaction, jets, or neutrinos.
analysis.result: For $Z_\odot/3$ models with $M_{\rm init}=11$–$21\,M_\odot$, fixed $E_{\rm kin}=1.2\times10^{51}\,\mathrm{erg}$, and $M(^{56}\mathrm{Ni})=0.07$–$0.08\,M_\odot$, late-time metallicity effects are weak. $[{\rm O\,I}]\,\lambda\lambda 6300.3,6363.8$ rises from 11 to $17\,M_\odot$ and then falls for $M_{\rm init}\gtrsim17$–$19\,M_\odot$; th11 and th21 have similar line fluxes despite O yields of $0.32$ versus $2.58\,M_\odot$. Assigning 90% of C/O-shell cooling to CO lowers the line by $\sim10$–$20\%$ and can underestimate $M_{\rm init}$ by $\sim1\,M_\odot$. Without strong CO/SiO cooling, $13\,M_\odot$ (O yield $0.79\,M_\odot$) fits best. $\gamma$-rays are fully trapped at 200 d, but by 800 d only $\sim20\%$ (th11) to $\sim50\%$ (th21) of the decay power is absorbed; th13 has $\tau_{\rm es}=1.28\rightarrow0.011$ and $L\sim10^{41}\rightarrow10^{38}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$. Dust, not smooth $\gamma$-ray leakage, explains the post-500 d excess fading of $\sim1.5\,\mathrm{mag}$: $0.1\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ silicates with $M_{\rm d}=10^{-4}$, $4\times10^{-3}$, and $5\times10^{-3}\,M_\odot$ at 600, 700, and 800 d, placed at $v<2000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, keep the $V$ offset within $0.2\,\mathrm{mag}$ and are optically thick from the UV through the IR.

analysis.problem: The work asks which progenitor mass is allowed by the nebular spectra of SN 1987A and whether the post-500 d optical deficit and UV behavior come from $\gamma$-ray leakage, molecular cooling, newly formed internal dust, or background-star contamination, rather than from circumstellar interaction.
analysis.method: One-dimensional, time-dependent NLTE radiative transfer with CMFGEN uses shuffled-shell macroscopic mixing and no microscopic mixing. The only power source is radioactive decay, dominated by the $^{56}\mathrm{Ni}$ chain, with nonlocal $\gamma$-ray deposition at gray opacity $\kappa_\gamma=0.06\,Y_e\,\mathrm{cm^{2}\,g^{-1}}$. Molecules are omitted in the global solution; a CO test retains only 10% of the C/O-shell absorbed decay power. After $\sim500\,\mathrm{d}$, $0.1\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ silicate dust is added only inside the metal-rich region at $v<2000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Spectra are placed at $D=49.59\,\mathrm{kpc}$ with $E(B-V)=0.15\,\mathrm{mag}$, and model comparisons are normalized by absorbed decay power.
assumptions: The $^{56}$Ni decay chain dominates the radioactive power at all modeled epochs, and $^{56}$Ni bubbles and CSM interaction are omitted.
limits: Late-time metallicity variations have only a relatively weak spectral effect.

analysis.reason: This radiative Kerr-magnetosphere GRPIC study is useful for relativistic-jet launching and compact-object VHE emission because it quantifies current closure and gamma-ray output relative to the Blandford–Znajek power, but it is peripheral to FRB, pulsar-wind, and supernova-engine problems.
analysis.result: A polar spark gap and a variable equatorial current sheet jointly sustain the global poloidal current. With low pair multiplicity, synchrotron–curvature (SC) cooling leaves the overall structure largely unchanged but drives spark-gap electric-field oscillations; polar and equatorial variability have no significant cross-correlation and $\Delta t\sim l_{\rm rec}/(\mathcal{R}_{\rm in}c)\sim 10\,r_{\rm g}/c$ at $\mathcal{R}_{\rm in}\sim +0.1$. Post-processed bolometric luminosities are $L_{\rm IC}\sim 10^{-4}L_{\rm BZ}$ and $L_{\rm SC}\sim 10^{-2}L_{\rm BZ}$ (reported in the opening summary as SC up to $\sim 1\%$ and inverse Compton $\sim 0.1\%$ of the BZ luminosity), with spark-gap photons reaching sub-TeV energies. Balancing $t_{\rm SC}=6\pi m_{\rm e}c/(\sigma_{\rm T}f_{\perp,\rm eff}^{2}B_{0}^{2}\Gamma)$ and $t_{\rm acc}\approx\Gamma m_{\rm e}c/(ef_{D}B_{0})$ gives $\Gamma_{\rm max}=\sqrt{f_{D}/f_{\perp,\rm eff}^{2}}\,\Gamma_{\rm SC}\simeq 3.7\times 10^{6}$ for representative equatorial $B_{0}\sim 10^{2}\,\mathrm{G}$.
analysis.problem: The paper investigates how a polar spark gap and an equatorial current sheet jointly close the global poloidal current in a radiative, charge-starved Kerr black-hole magnetosphere, and how SC cooling changes particle acceleration, variability, and gamma-ray signatures relative to observed VHE flares.
analysis.method: The study uses axisymmetric 2D GRPIC in Kerr–Schild 3+1 form, evolving $\frac{1}{c}\partial_t\bm{B}=-\nabla\times\bm{E}$ and $\frac{1}{c}\partial_t\bm{D}=\nabla\times\bm{H}-\frac{4\pi}{c}\bm{J}$ with Hamiltonian particles, ambient-photon inverse Compton scattering, and two-photon pair creation. It compares no cooling, $\Gamma_{\rm SC}=\infty$, with marginal slow cooling, $\Gamma_{\rm SC}=800$, from a Wald vertical field at $a=0.99$, $\tilde{B}_{0}=5\times 10^{3}$, $\varepsilon_{0}=5\times 10^{-2}$, and $\tau_{0}=10$ ($\sigma_{0}\simeq 1.2\times 10^{4}$), followed by ray tracing. The SC drag is $\bm{g}\simeq-\frac{2}{3}\frac{e^{4}}{m_{\rm e}^{2}c^{4}}\Gamma^{2}\bm{\beta}B_{\perp,\rm eff}^{2}$.
assumptions: The adopted plasma supply has a low pair multiplicity, explicitly described as a low-pair-multiplicity parameter choice.
limits: Synthetic luminosity-variation amplitudes are smaller than the order-of-magnitude enhancements in prominent VHE flares.

analysis.research_progress: At low multiplicity, radiative cooling is an incremental correction to force-free current closure: the parabolic near-horizon geometry and global circuit persist, while pair-production efficiency causes gap oscillations. Both regions vary on $\Delta t\lesssim 10\,r_{\rm g}/c$, but only the polar region shows a distinct oscillation peak and their cross-correlation is insignificant. The radiative yields satisfy $L_{\rm SC}\sim 10^{-2}L_{\rm BZ}$ and $L_{\rm IC}\sim 10^{-4}L_{\rm BZ}$, with slow- and fast-cooling spectra $\Gamma dN/d\Gamma\propto\Gamma^{0}$ and $\propto\Gamma^{-1}$.

analysis.reason: The paper quantifies when downstream second-order Fermi acceleration at SNR shocks can reshape cosmic-ray spectra and the associated pp gamma-ray flux, which is useful for supernova-shock and high-energy studies, but it does not treat central engines, shock breakout, FRBs, or jets.
analysis.result: Stochastic acceleration appreciably changes the downstream particle spectrum whenever $\eta \gtrsim \xi_{\rm CR}$. For standard Model I parameters, including stochastic acceleration and wave feedback increases the gamma-ray flux between $\sim 1$ and $100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ by $\sim 50\%$. For an undamped $f(p)\propto p^{-4}$ Kolmogorov cascade, $P t_{\rm age}/P_{\rm CR}\approx (3/4)\eta/\xi_{\rm CR}$; acceleration times scale as $\tau_{\rm acc}\sim p^{1/3}$ (Kolmogorov) or $\sim p^{1/2}$ (Kraichnan), while source-free inertial spectra are $W\sim k^{-5/3}$ and $W\sim k^{-3/2}$. Upstream self-generated waves alone do not significantly modify the downstream spectrum because the cascade rapidly removes their energy.
analysis.reading_entry: Evolution of Turbulence and Stochastic Acceleration Downstream
analysis.problem: The paper asks whether particles accelerated at an SNR shock and then advected downstream have their spectrum modified by second-order Fermi acceleration, and whether that change appears in $pp\to\pi^0$ gamma rays, despite strong-shock DSA spectra being nearly universal for $M_s\gg 1$.
analysis.method: The particle distribution and turbulent spectrum are evolved together through $\partial_t f=p^{-2}\partial_p(p^2 D_{pp}\partial_p f)$ and $\partial_t W+\partial_k F=-\Gamma W+S-D$, using quasi-linear $D_{pp}$, resonant damping $\Gamma$, and Kolmogorov or Kraichnan cascades. The SNR downstream is split into independent shells with adiabatic losses, and the $pp$ gamma-ray flux is integrated with Naima and Kafexhiu cross sections, comparing cases with and without stochastic acceleration and wave feedback.

analysis.reason: The paper is relevant to supernova and compact-merger neutrino transport because collisional flavor conversion need not settle to an attracting fixed point, and the resulting cycles or chaos shift time-averaged flavor populations. It is worth knowing rather than essential because it is a specialized kinetic bifurcation study, not a direct engine or high-energy observational constraint.
analysis.result: Homogeneous collective precession (HCP) is a rotating-frame fixed point, but it is not always attracting. As the electron collision rate $\kappa_e$ approaches $0.0025$ from below, the target growth rate and the HCP number offset vanish together (supercritical Hopf); near $\kappa_e\simeq0.018$ a finite-amplitude pair appears, and the unstable branch merges with the target near $\kappa_e\simeq0.0221$ (subcritical Hopf). An independent HCP crossing occurs at $\kappa_e\simeq0.0200194578$, before target destabilization at $\kappa_e\simeq0.0221481171$. For $0.034\le\kappa_e\le0.060$, successive maxima of $P_z$ period-double eight times toward a stable $256$-cycle, with spacing ratios approaching $\delta_{\rm F}\simeq4.669$. At $\kappa_e=0.055025$ the leading Lyapunov estimate is $\widehat\lambda_1\simeq2.8\times10^{-3}$ for bounded irregular evolution. The HCP balance is $s(u^\star)^2=z^\star\tau^\star$, while averages obey $s[\langle u\rangle_T^2+\mathrm{Var}_T(u)]=\langle z\rangle_T\langle Z\rangle_T+\mathrm{Cov}_T(z,Z)-\tfrac12\mathcal{B}_{u^2}$. The largest reported HCP-versus-time-average population deviation is $8.03\%$, set by the mean coherent torque rather than by stationarity.
analysis.problem: The issue is whether a collisionally balanced HCP state attracts neutrino flavor trajectories or whether collisional flavor instability instead produces Hopf cycles, period doubling, and chaos, and how far HCP or mean-only estimates miss the time-averaged flavor populations.
analysis.method: The full quantum kinetic equations are linearized in the rotating frame, including the response of the self-interaction field; after removal of the common phase, local attraction requires all seven Jacobian eigenvalues to have negative real parts. For energy-independent rates the collective matrix follows the monochromatic kinetics and residuals contract at least as $e^{-\kappa_* t}$. Root number is fixed by the sign of $\mathcal{C}$, and $\kappa_e$ is scanned with multiple shooting and Lyapunov estimates. Steady balance is $s(u^\star)^2=z^\star\tau^\star$, whereas the time-averaged identity keeps $\mathrm{Var}_T(u)$ and $\mathrm{Cov}_T(z,Z)$.
assumptions: Existence of an HCP state does not imply attraction; attraction is judged by linearizing the full quantum kinetic equations in the rotating frame, including self-interaction response.
limits: Because of fluctuation and coherent-torque terms, an HCP estimate need not equal the time average; the maximum reported deviation is $8.03\%$, and relative spectral errors also depend on $c_E$.

analysis.reason: The paper establishes an intrinsic hard X-ray point-source excess in the Nuclear Stellar Disk and associates it with high-mass white-dwarf intermediate polars and possibly millisecond pulsars, which is relevant compact-object high-energy context but not central to FRB, jet, neutrino, or supernova-engine studies.
analysis.result: Within the NSD ($|l|\lesssim 1.3^{\circ}$, $|b|\lesssim 0.3^{\circ}$), XMM-Newton finds a concentration of intrinsically hard point sources. Plane sources are softer, with mean $\mathrm{HR}\simeq 0.1$ (PN) and $\simeq-0.3$ (MOS), where $\mathrm{HR}\equiv(H-S)/(H+S)$, $H=4.5$–$12\,\mathrm{keV}$, and $S=2.0$–$4.5\,\mathrm{keV}$. Inside-versus-outside HR distributions differ at $>8\sigma$. At $-1.05^{\circ}<l<0.55^{\circ}$, observed $\mathrm{HR}\gtrsim 0.3$ exceeds $\mathrm{HR}<0.2$ predicted for $5\times10^{22}<N_{\rm H}<8\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$. Hard and soft longitude/latitude distributions differ at $>12\sigma/9\sigma$ ($p=2\times10^{-35}/3\times10^{-20}$). Scale heights are $h_{l,\rm s}=2^{\circ}$ ($\sim280\,\mathrm{pc}$), $h_{b,\rm s}=0.31^{\circ}$ ($\sim44\,\mathrm{pc}$), $h_{l,\rm h}=0.66^{\circ}$ ($\sim90\,\mathrm{pc}$), and $h_{b,\rm h}=0.17^{\circ}$ ($\sim24\,\mathrm{pc}$). The stellar-mass distribution follows the soft sources better than the hard sources. The hard NSD population most likely consists of intermediate polars with high $M_{\rm WD}$, possibly plus MSPs; representative partial covering at $kT=36\,\mathrm{keV}$ gives $\mathrm{HR}\sim0.82$ versus $\sim0.36$ without it, and $\langle kT\rangle\approx34\,\mathrm{keV}$ for IPs versus $\approx11\,\mathrm{keV}$ for polars. The $\log N$–$\log S$ slope is $\alpha\sim1.35$–$1.5$.
analysis.problem: The paper tests whether the hard X-ray point-source concentration overlapping the NSD is an intrinsically harder compact-object population or only an artifact of large line-of-sight $N_{\rm H}$, and what that population implies for the unresolved sources underlying the Galactic-center and Galactic-ridge X-ray emission.
analysis.method: Using the XMM-Newton Heritage Survey and cleaned 4XMM-DR14 sources over $|l|<10^{\circ}$, $|b|<1^{\circ}$, the authors compare $\mathrm{HR}\equiv(H-S)/(H+S)$ inside and outside the NSD with count-rate and exposure-matched K–S tests. Outflow suppresses radiative feedback as $f_\beta\propto(1-\beta)^2$. The discussion gives $\delta\approx 1.56$, $L\approx 0.3L_{\rm iso}$, $\ell=35.4(L_{\rm iso}/0.5\%L_{\rm Edd})(r_g/R)$, $t_{\rm IC}=0.03(R/r_g)R/c$, $B_{\rm eq}\approx 1.1\times 10^{7}(R/r_g)^{-1}\,\mathrm{G}$, $\sigma\approx 6.9(R/r_g)^{-1}$ and $v_A\approx 0.9c$, favoring a pair corona. The IXPE polarization-angle difference is $3.3^\circ\pm 3.2^\circ$; requiring the band-to-band Faraday difference to be $<0.11$ rad yields $\eta_\Delta<0.14(B_\parallel/10^{7}\,\mathrm{G})^{-1}$.

analysis.problem: Static Comptonizing coronae underpredict the hard-state polarization of Cyg X-1: IXPE finds about $4\%$ polarization parallel to the radio jet, while static models give only $1$–$2.5\%$. analysis.method: polrad-3D Monte Carlo polarized transfer is run in a three-dimensional cylinder with the symmetry axis along $z$, temporarily neglecting general relativity. Continuity gives $n(z)\propto\beta^{-1}$, with Thomson depths $t_z=\bar{n}\sigma_T H$ and $t_r=\bar{n}\sigma_T R$. Constant-$\beta$ and accelerating profiles from $\beta_0=0.1$ to $\beta_{\rm top}$ are compared for a $100\,\mathrm{keV}$ Maxwell–Jüttner plasma and unpolarized isotropic $10\,\mathrm{eV}$ cyclo-synchrotron seeds, using invariant optical depth and the full Klein–Nishina Fano matrix. Grids in $t_z$ and $\beta_{\rm top}$, with up to $6.4\times 10^8$ photons, are matched to $\Gamma=1.6$ and $q=4\%$ at $i=27.5^\circ$.
assumptions: The radial scale is taken to be $R\sim r_g$ because the flow is unlikely to concentrate the required energy into much smaller regions.
limits: Only $h\leq 0.8$ with $\beta_{\rm top}=0.5$–$0.9$ jointly fits $\Gamma=1.6$ and $4\%$ polarization; larger $h$ remains below $4\%$ even at $\beta_{\rm top}=0.99$.

analysis.result: An energy-resolved kinetic treatment gives a damping time of 2.7 s for a 1 kHz, 10 km oscillation at nuclear density and 4 MeV, against 19 ms for freely escaping neutrinos. For remnant kHz modes the composition is nearly frozen, so the Urca channel damps them on seconds rather than tens of milliseconds; sampled DD2 states give mean capture energies 19–46 MeV and emission-weighted absorption lengths below 7 m. analysis.problem: Transparent Urca bulk viscosity was expected to damp neutron-star-merger density oscillations within tens of milliseconds when the relaxation rate matches the mode frequency, but that estimate treats only thermal-energy neutrinos as free-streaming and omits reabsorption of much harder sub-threshold capture neutrinos.
analysis.method: DD2 $npe\mu$ matter is evolved at fixed cold $\beta$-equilibrium composition with direct Urca from momentum-resolved phase space, modified Urca in the Fermi-surface approximation, and isotropic elastic neutral-current scattering. Linear energy-resolved kinetics define an admittance $\Lambda(\omega,k)$, effective bulk viscosity $\zeta_{\rm eff}(\omega,k)=C^{2}{\rm Re}\Lambda/|-i\omega+B\Lambda|^{2}$, and damping time $\tau=K_T/(\zeta_{\rm eff}\omega^{2})$, using $C=n(\partial\Delta\mu/\partial n)_{T,Y_e,Y_\mu}$, $B=-(\partial\Delta\mu/\partial n_e)_{n,T,Y_\mu}$, and $K_T=n(\partial p/\partial n)_{T,Y_e,Y_\mu}$.
assumptions: Muonic reactions are not included, and the muon fraction is held fixed during the oscillation.
limits: The kinetic damping time cannot be shorter than $\tau_{\rm res}=2K_{T}B/(C^{2}\omega)$, and every computed time lies above that bound.

analysis.reason: This directly constrains the circumgalactic contribution to FRB dispersion measure using the second CHIME/FRB baseband catalog, including a radial and mass-dependent DM stack relevant to FRB sightline environments.
analysis.result: Within $D_L\le50\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ and one virial radius, the mean excess is $119\pm44\,\mathrm{pc\,cm^{-3}}$ ($p=0.0053$, about $2.6\sigma$). Across 628 intersections to $150\,\mathrm{Mpc}$, mean DM tentatively declines with impact parameter ($p=0.0046$, about $2.6\sigma$), mainly for $10\le\log(M_*/M_\odot)\le11$. The adopted CGM scaling is $n_e^{\mathrm{CGM}}(r)\propto r^{-3\beta}$, with extrapolated $n_{e,0}=(1.7-21.1)\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ and $\beta=0.68^{+0.15}_{-0.16}$. The excess peaks near $\sim90\pm75\,\mathrm{pc\,cm^{-3}}$ at $0.2\lesssim b_{\min}/r_{\rm CGM}\lesssim0.4$, whereas large-scale structure contributes only about $14\pm39\,\mathrm{pc\,cm^{-3}}$.
analysis.problem: The paper tests whether foreground galaxy CGM halos produce an extragalactic FRB DM excess and whether its radial behavior traces CGM baryons rather than large-scale structure or host-galaxy cross-matching.
analysis.method: BaseCat2 contains 2086 bursts and 1748 independent sources, stacked on foreground halos using $\mathrm{DM}=\int_0^z n_e(z')(1+z')^{-1}dl$ and $\Delta\mathrm{DM}_{\mathrm{egal}}=\mathrm{DM}-\mathrm{DM}_{\mathrm{MW}}$. The radial analysis uses $b_{\min}/r_{\rm CGM}$, Gaussian bin-membership weights, and the fit $n_e^{\rm CGM}(r)=n_{e,0}[1+(r/r_c)^2]^{-3\beta/2}$. SLOW and Simba comparisons test alternative contributions, while $\eta_{\mathrm{CGM}}=\mathrm{DM}_{\mathrm{CGM}}/\mathrm{DM}_{\mathrm{cosmic}}$ forecasts favorable redshifts.
assumptions: Because DM_CGM and DM_cosmic are drawn from different simulations, they are treated as statistically independent.

analysis.reason: This study performs 3D SPH simulations to investigate the hydrodynamic Tug-boat mechanism and black hole natal kicks in core-collapse supernovae, providing critical physical limits on whether natal kicks can tilt binary orbits to produce negative effective inspiral spins $\chi_{\rm eff} < 0$.
analysis.result: Asymmetric fallback accretion drives the Tug-boat mechanism, where high explosion energies ($E_{\rm SN} \ge 0.6 E_{\rm bin}$) amplify final kick velocities above symmetric expectations ($v_{\rm Tug} \equiv v_f / v_{\rm sym} > 1$, reaching $v_{\rm Tug} \sim 2$ for $28\,M_\odot$ and $34\,M_\odot$), while low energies suppress kicks ($v_{\rm Tug} \sim 0.2$). Even extreme retro-orbital kicks with $v_{\rm kick} \sim 1000\ \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}}$ cannot consistently flip orbital orientation or produce persistent negative $\chi_{\rm eff}$. Although post-SN semi-major axes match Instantaneous Mass Loss (IML) calculations within $\le 10\%$, orbital eccentricities deviate by up to $\sim 60\%$, strongly shifting gravitational-wave merger timescales governed by $\frac{dE}{dt} = -\frac{32G^4}{5c^5}\frac{M_{\rm bh1}M_{\rm bh2}M}{a^5}f(e)$.

analysis.problem: Whether hydrodynamic natal kicks and asymmetric fallback accretion in core-collapse supernovae can tilt binary black hole orbital angular momentum sufficiently to generate negative effective inspiral spin parameters $\chi_{\rm eff} < 0$, and whether the Instantaneous Mass Loss (IML) approximation accurately reproduces post-explosion binary orbital parameters and coalescence times.
analysis.method: Performed 3D SPH hydrodynamic simulations with modified GADGET using stripped helium star progenitor models ($13\,M_\odot, 21\,M_\odot, 28\,M_\odot, 34\,M_\odot$), where central core collapse forms a sink particle with initial mass $M_{\rm bh,2,i} = 3\,M_\odot$ and initial spin $S_{\rm BH} = 0$, accreting SPH particles satisfying $r < r_{\rm acc} = 0.01\,R_\odot$ and $j < j_{\rm isco}$; asymmetric explosion energy $E_{\rm SN}/E_{\rm bin} \in [0.2, 0.9]$ is injected according to the angular profile $f(\theta,\Delta,\sigma) = 1 + \Delta e^{-\theta^2/2\sigma^2}$.
assumptions: All simulations begin with an initially non-rotating black hole sink particle ($S_{\rm BH}=0$).
limits: Even natal kicks of order $\sim 1000\ \mathrm{km/s}$ cannot consistently invert orbital angular momentum to produce negative $\chi_{\rm eff}$.

analysis.reason: This work establishes an exact angular moment framework for neutrino pair annihilation around black hole accretion discs and uncovers a fundamental general relativistic sign-reversal effect on flavour conversion, directly relevant to compact object central engines and relativistic jet launching in GRBs.
analysis.result: In Kerr spacetime with spin $a = 0.99$, $T_x = T_e$, and $T_{\bar{e}} = 1.5 T_e$, equipartition flavour conversion reduces annihilation energy deposition by $54\%$ in flat spacetime but increases it by $+11\%$ in Kerr spacetime. This sign reversal is driven by cross pairs between the inner ring and outer disc: general relativity amplifies outer-outer pairs by a factor of $2.0$, but amplifies cross pairs by $6.3\text{--}7.4\times$, elevating cross pairs to $0.77$ of the total Kerr deposition (compared to $0.23$ in flat spacetime). In the exact separability limit ($f_{\nu_x} = f_{\bar{\nu}_x} = 0$), the ratio is $\mathcal{R} = (1-P)(1-\bar{P}) + \frac{D_x}{2D_e} P \bar{P} = 0.159$ at $P = \bar{P} = 2/3$ (a $6.3\times$ suppression). Gravitational redistribution concentrates energy deposition: $50\%$ of $\dot{E}_{\infty}$ originates from $r < 10M$, $90\%$ from $r < 20M$, and $73\%$ within $5M$ above the disc plane.
analysis.problem: Whether neutrino pair annihilation $\nu\bar{\nu} \to e^+ e^-$ in curved spacetime can deposit sufficient energy to power relativistic jets in gamma-ray bursts, and whether general relativistic transport effects (gravitational redshift, ray bending, and frame dragging) and neutrino flavour conversion can be decoupled when electron and heavy-lepton neutrinospheres are spatially segregated.
analysis.method: Exact angular moment factorisation decomposing the local energy deposition rate $\dot{q} = \frac{D G_F^2}{3\pi c^5} [\mathcal{M}(\mathcal{E}_4, \bar{\mathcal{E}}_3) + \mathcal{M}(\mathcal{E}_3, \bar{\mathcal{E}}_4)]$ and momentum deposition rate $c\dot{p}_i = \frac{D G_F^2}{3\pi c^5} [\mathcal{P}_i(\mathcal{E}_4, \bar{\mathcal{E}}_3) + \mathcal{P}_i(\bar{\mathcal{E}}_4, \mathcal{E}_3)]$ into 20 direction moments (ranks 0 to 3, with 16 independent) defined by $\mathcal{E}_n(\boldsymbol{\Omega}) = \int_0^\infty f \varepsilon^n \mathrm{d}\varepsilon$, coupled to the open-source code ANNIHILUS utilizing OpenMP C backward ray tracing with 4th-order Runge-Kutta in Mino time and edge-adapted quadrature.
assumptions: Neutrinos free-stream along null geodesics outside neutrinospheres without scattering or re-absorption.
limits: Neglects neutrino re-absorption and pair production opacity within dense outflows.

analysis.result: In the low-hard state of Cygnus X-1, modeling reproduces the observed $2\text{--}8\ \mathrm{keV}$ polarization degree of $\sim 4\%$ (IXPE) and $\sim 5\%$ (XL-Calibur) aligned parallel to the radio jet, favoring a radially extended wedge-like corona over a lamppost geometry. analysis.reason: This paper investigates whether quasi-spherical fallback in binary neutron star mergers can power secondary relativistic jets for extended emission while simultaneously choking them, directly addressing central engines, relativistic jets, and breakout physics.
analysis.result: The fate of the secondary jet is governed by the dimensionless luminosity $\widetilde{L} \propto f_{\rm circ}/(\xi_{\rm pol}\theta_{j}^{2})$, defining jet-dominated, cocoon-dominated, and choked breakout regimes. For non-promptly captured fallback fraction $f_{\rm npc} \simeq 0.52$ and circularization fractions $f_{\rm circ} \in [0.052, 0.52]$, jets with $\theta_j \le 0.3\ \mathrm{rad}$ avoid being choked when $f_{\rm circ} \gtrsim 0.08$. Furthermore, radioactive $r$-process heating has local temperature $T_{\rm local} \approx (4\text{--}5)T_{\rm eff}$, overestimating luminosity by $(T_{\rm local}/T_{\rm eff})^4 \sim 10^2\text{--}10^3$; accounting for optical diffusion, nuclear heating yields only $L_{\rm EE} \sim 10^{43}\text{--}10^{44}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, insufficient to power observed short GRB extended emission.
analysis.problem: Whether quasi-spherical fallback accretion in binary neutron star mergers can provide sufficient fuel to power observed short GRB extended emission without choking the secondary relativistic jet in the refilled polar ejecta, and whether pure $r$-process radioactive heating can account for extended emission energetics.
analysis.method: A semi-analytic dynamical model coupled to GRMHD post-processing: fallback accretion follows $\dot{M}_{\rm FB}(t) = \dot{M}_0 t^{-5/3}$, driving secondary jet power $L_j(t) = \eta_j \dot{M}_{\rm circ}(t)c^2 = \eta_j f_{\rm circ}\dot{M}_{\rm FB}(t)c^2$ with $\eta_j = 0.1$. The polar ambient density is $\rho_{\rm pol}(r,t) = \xi_{\rm pol}\rho_{\rm FB}(r,t)$, yielding dimensionless luminosity $\widetilde{L}(t,r_h) = \frac{L_j(t)}{\Sigma_j(r_h)\rho_{\rm pol}(r_h,t)c^3} \propto \frac{f_{\rm circ}}{\xi_{\rm pol}\theta_j^2}$ and head velocity $\beta_h = \frac{1 + \widetilde{L}^{-1/2}\beta_a}{1 + \widetilde{L}^{-1/2}}$, with equivalent isotropic X-ray energy computed via $E_{X,\rm iso}^{\rm NT} = \frac{\eta_X}{f_j}\int L_j(t)\,dt$.
assumptions: The bound merger ejecta continues to fall back toward the central remnant in an approximately quasi-spherical configuration with $\dot{M}_{\rm FB} \propto t^{-5/3}$.
limits: Fallback properties depend on specific microphysical GRMHD simulations and would be altered if the merger remnant is a long-lived neutron star.

analysis.research_progress: Demonstrates the dual role of quasi-spherical fallback as both fuel and obstacle for secondary jets, rules out pure $r$-process heating for extended emission due to large optical depth and diffusion losses, and determines the critical unchoking condition $f_{\rm circ} \gtrsim 0.08$ for relativistic jets.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic illustration of the fallback-fed secondary-jet model and possible outcome scenarios. The bound merger ejecta continues to fall back toward the central remnant in an approximately quasi-spherical configuration shown in blue. A fraction of this material circularizes and forms an accretion torus, thereby powering a secondary jet, while fallback along the polar direction partially refills the funnel previously cleared by the prompt jet and impedes its propagation. Depending on the competition between the jet power and the density of the polar fallback material, three outcomes are possible: a jet-dominated breakout (left), where the secondary jet successfully penetrates the fallback envelope; a cocoon-dominated breakout (middle), where stronger jet–fallback interaction transfers a substantial fraction of the secondary-jet energy into the surrounding cocoon; and a choked jet (right), where the jet-tail catches up with the jet-head before a successful breakout is achieved.
figures.label: Fig. 1

The color scale shows the dimensionless jet-head luminosity $\log_{10}\widetilde{L}_{\rm cross}$ evaluated at the crossing time and the black dashed line shows the curve for $\widetilde{L}_{\rm cross}=1$. The gray region denotes choked jets with $t_{\rm jet,cross}\leq 0$. All other model parameters are fixed at the values listed in Table 1.

analysis.reason: The paper investigates the first observational candidate for a hierarchical triple black hole merger pair (GW230729_082317 and GW231118_005626) in LVK O4a, providing valuable empirical constraints on compact object mergers and dynamical assembly in dense environments.
analysis.result: For candidate pair GW230729_082317 and GW231118_005626, joint Bayesian parameter estimation yields a Bayes factor $\mathcal{B} = 110$ favoring the hierarchical triple merger hypothesis, but accounting for low prior probability reduces the posterior odds ratio to $\mathcal{O} \approx 0.1$. The 1G remnant mass ($M_{\rm rem} \approx 19.4\,M_\odot$) matches the 2G primary mass ($m_1 \sim 2m_2$) with overlapping sky localization and distance ($d_L \sim 1630\,\mathrm{Mpc}$). Under a Poisson process with delay distribution $P(\Delta < T) \propto (T/t_{\rm max})^\alpha$, the $90\%$ upper limit on the local event rate density is $R_0 \in [4.2, 75.3]\,\mathrm{Gpc^{-3}\,yr^{-1}}$ for null detection, and $R_0 \in [4.1, 95.1]\,\mathrm{Gpc^{-3}\,yr^{-1}}$ ($t_{\rm max} = 10\,\mathrm{yr}$) if confirmed.

analysis.reason: This work is relevant to compact object high-energy astrophysics and jet-accretion scaling relations, developing a rigorous forward-modeling framework to test intermediate-mass black holes in dwarf galaxies using the radio/X-ray Fundamental Plane.
analysis.result: For a $10^{6}\,M_{\odot}$ black hole point source at a $5\sigma$ threshold, current VLBA detection probabilities are $4.9\times 10^{-5}\text{--}0.029$ (ID 26), $0.03\text{--}0.06$ (ID 82), and $0.08\text{--}0.17$ (ID 83). Reaching $50\%$ completeness requires rms sensitivity $\sigma_{50}$ of $0.10\text{--}0.76\,\mu\mathrm{Jy\,beam^{-1}}$ (ID 26), $0.77\text{--}1.67\,\mu\mathrm{Jy\,beam^{-1}}$ (ID 82), and $3.37\text{--}8.31\,\mu\mathrm{Jy\,beam^{-1}}$ (ID 83). Extended structure attenuation scales as $\eta_{\theta}^{-1} = 1 + (\theta_s / \theta_b)^2$, which attenuates peak flux by factors of $\sim 13$, $33$, and $29$ for a $5\,\mathrm{pc}$ source.
analysis.problem: Radio non-detections cannot be directly inverted into physical black hole mass upper limits because spatial filtering across intermediate physical scales ($\sim 1\text{--}100\,\mathrm{pc}$) between VLA and VLBA baselines, beam dilution, non-simultaneous variability, and astrometric offsets conflate non-detections with resolved-out flux or false host associations.
analysis.method: A forward probabilistic framework is formulated using the Fundamental Plane relation $\ell_{R} = \xi_{RX}\ell_{X} + \mu_{\rm FP}m + b_{0}$ with Merloni calibration $(\xi_{RX},\mu_{\rm FP},b_0)=(0.60,0.78,7.33)$, where $\ell_R \equiv \log[\nu L_\nu(5\,\mathrm{GHz})/\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}]$, $\ell_X \equiv \log[L_{2-10\,\mathrm{keV}}/\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}]$, and $m \equiv \log(M_\bullet/M_\odot)$. The non-detection probability is computed via $P_{\rm nd}(m) = \int d\alpha\, d\ell_X\, d\ell_R\; p(\alpha)p(\ell_X)\mathcal{N}(\ell_R;\bar{\ell}_R,\sigma_R)\Phi\left[\frac{n_\sigma\sigma - \eta_\theta S_9(\ell_R,\alpha)}{\sigma}\right]$, incorporating beam dilution $\eta_\theta = \theta_b^2/(\theta_b^2+\theta_s^2)$, intrinsic scatter $\sigma_R$, and spectral index marginalization.
assumptions: A radio/X-ray Fundamental Plane test is valid only when compact radio emission, hard X-rays, accretion state, and host association refer to the same central accretor.
limits: Deeper integration alone cannot recover source structure that is resolved out by the chosen interferometric baselines.

analysis.reason: This paper presents multi-decadal X-ray timing observations of the accreting pulsar Hercules X-1, offering valuable observational constraints on compact object superorbital period evolution and neutron star precession.
analysis.result: The analysis finds that the superorbital period of Her X-1 is $P_{\rm sup} = 35.1(1)\text{ d}$ and exhibits a long-term secular decay rate of $\dot{P}_{\rm sup} = -4.7(1)\times 10^{-5}\text{ s s}^{-1}$ (with epoch folding yielding $\dot{P}_{\rm sup} = -5(2)\times 10^{-5}\text{ s s}^{-1}$), corresponding to a decay timescale of $P_{\rm sup}/|\dot{P}_{\rm sup}| \sim 1918\text{ yr}$; superimposed wanders on timescales of $10\text{--}38$ cycles show up to $\sim 5\%$ variation and correlate with X-ray count rate (Pearson $r = 0.73$).
analysis.problem: Investigating whether the $\sim 35\text{ d}$ superorbital modulation in Hercules X-1 represents white-noise wandering around a fixed mean or a secular decay, and probing the physical mechanism between radiation-driven warped disc precession and neutron star free precession.
analysis.method: Constructed a 30-to-50-year continuous light curve combining CGRO/BATSE, RXTE/ASM, Swift/BAT, Fermi/GBM, and MAXI/GSC; performed an epoch folding search in $P_{\rm sup}\text{--}\dot{P}_{\rm sup}$ parameter space, and modeled main-on peak arrivals with quadratic $O-C$ fitting using $O_n = C_0 + n P_{\rm sup} + \frac{n^2}{2!} P_{\rm sup} \dot{P}_{\rm sup}$.
assumptions: The neutron star behaves as a biaxial body ($I_3 < I_2 = I_1$) undergoing free precession about $I_3$.

analysis.reason: This is a low-latency BNS early-warning search method for third-generation detectors, useful for compact-object multi-messenger follow-up, but it does not directly study FRB/PRS, supernova engines, jets, neutrinos, or circumstellar interaction.
analysis.result: A CNN with $\mathcal{N}=10^{3}$ templates reaches a sensitivity distance comparable to SFT matched filtering, which instead needs approximately $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=10^{7}$ templates, about four orders of magnitude more. For $f_{\max}=10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $f_{\min}\in\{2,3,4,5\}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, the quoted evaluation time falls from minutes to milliseconds, a speed-up of about $1.6\times10^{4}$–$4.0\times10^{4}$; the CNN per-template cost is $\langle\mathfrak{c}_1\rangle\approx(3$–$25)\,\mu\mathrm{s}$. At fixed template number, sensitivity follows $\langle s\rangle\sim\rho_{\rm opt}^{2}(1-\langle\mu\rangle)$ with $\rho_{\rm opt}^{2}\propto\int_{f_{\min}}^{10\,\mathrm{Hz}}f^{-7/3}/S_n(f)\,df$.
analysis.problem: Early warning of binary neutron-star inspirals in third-generation detectors is limited by the computing cost of evaluating the detection statistic at low latency.
analysis.method: Early inspirals are represented by narrowband SFTs with $T_{\mathrm{SFT}}=31\,\mathrm{s}$ and $\Delta k=51$ bins about $f(t;\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}})=f_{\max}[1+(256/5)(\pi f_{\max})^{8/3}(G\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}}/c^{3})^{5/3}(t_{\max}-t)]^{-3/8}$. A CNN minimizes binary cross-entropy and searches only $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}}$, while the SFT statistic $\mathcal{X}$ is maximized analytically over phase and luminosity distance and then over an eight-dimensional bank. Latency is modeled as $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{N}\langle\mathfrak{c}_1\rangle$, with $f_s=40\,\mathrm{Hz}$ for the 3, 4, and 5 Hz regimes.
limits: For lower chirp masses, evolution from $f_{\min}$ to $f_{\max}$ can exceed the fixed analysis window, so the signal is aligned at $f_{\max}$ and only its late portion is retained.

analysis.reason: This ZTF spectroscopic census of hydrogen-rich SLSNe directly constrains circumstellar interaction, pre-explosion mass loss, and possible Ia-CSM contamination, which are central to supernova-engine and CSM studies.
analysis.result: Of 106 hydrogen-rich SLSNe, 105 show narrow Balmer emission and are spectroscopically SLSNe-IIn; SN 2022lvm is the sole broad-lined SLSN-II in the discussed 2021–2022 subset comparison (1/36, 2.8%). Measured $L_{\mathrm{H}\alpha}$ spans $2.2\times10^{40}$ to $1.5\times10^{42}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ (median $2.6\times10^{41}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$). The median Balmer decrement rises from 2.85 before $+100$ d to 4.40 afterward, below the Ia-CSM comparison medians 6.58 and 17.76. After excluding the SLSN-II and six Ia-CSM-like objects, median shell speed correlates with peak magnitude ($r=0.63$, $p=0.010$): brighter events tend to have lower $v_{\rm s}$. For 13 calibrated objects at $v_{\rm CSM}=100\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ and $\epsilon=0.5$, $\dot{M}\sim0.028$–$0.30\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ from $L=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\dot{M}v_{\rm s}^{3}/u_{\rm w}$. Six of 105 narrow-line events ($\sim6\%$) are Ia-CSM-like. Narrow interaction lines can persist beyond $+200$ d, with no Balmer morphology unique to SLSNe-IIn relative to fainter SNe IIn.
analysis.problem: Whether luminous narrow-line SLSNe-IIn are spectroscopically only the bright extreme of SNe IIn, what dense hydrogen-rich CSM and enhanced pre-explosion mass loss they require, and whether narrow Balmer lines plus high luminosity uniquely imply core collapse rather than Ia-CSM.
analysis.method: The study uses 304 optical spectra of 106 ZTF events selected at rest-frame peak $M\leq-19.9$ mag, with phases $(t-t_{\rm peak})/(1+z)$ and fluxes scaled by $10^{-0.4(m_{\rm GP}-m_{\rm syn})}$ from Gaussian-process light curves (287 absolutely calibrated). Balmer luminosity, pEW and FWHM are measured after local continuum subtraction. Single-epoch Monte Carlo electron-scattering snapshots (escatter; $10^{5}$ H$\alpha$ photons outside a cold dense shell) fit line profiles. Mass-loss rates use $L=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\dot{M}\frac{v_{\rm s}^{3}}{u_{\rm w}}$ and $\dot{M}=\frac{2L}{\epsilon}\frac{u_{\rm w}}{v_{\rm s}^{3}}$, with luminosity integrated from the spectra and a blackbody extension to 3000–20000 Å.
assumptions: Quoted mass-loss rates use the adopted CSM-interaction model with $\epsilon=0.5$ and $v_{\rm CSM}=100\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, commonly with a shock speed of $5000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.
limits: Inferred mass-loss rates are order-of-magnitude estimates rather than precise progenitor mass-loss histories.

analysis.research_progress: The sample shows that SLSN-IIn H$\alpha$ pEW and FWHM overlap those of lower-luminosity SNe IIn, while lines persisting for tens to hundreds of days and $\dot{M}\sim0.028$–$0.30\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ exceed ordinary OB or red-supergiant winds under $L=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\dot{M}v_{\rm s}^{3}/u_{\rm w}$. Brighter events tend toward lower $v_{\rm s}$, consistent with denser or more massive CSM and higher radiative efficiency, and $\sim6\%$ of the narrow-line objects are Ia-CSM-like.

analysis.result: For $Z_\odot/3$ models with $M_{\rm init}=11$–$21\,M_\odot$, fixed $E_{\rm kin}=1.2\times10^{51}\,\mathrm{erg}$, and $M(^{56}\mathrm{Ni})=0.07$–$0.08\,M_\odot$, late-time metallicity effects are weak. $[{\rm O\,I}]\,\lambda\lambda 6300.3,6363.8$ rises from 11 to $17\,M_\odot$ and then falls for $M_{\rm init}\gtrsim17$–$19\,M_\odot$; th11 and th21 have similar line fluxes despite O yields of $0.32$ versus $2.58\,M_\odot$. Assigning 90% of C/O-shell cooling to CO lowers the line by $\sim10$–$20\%$ and can underestimate $M_{\rm init}$ by $\sim1\,M_\odot$. Without strong CO/SiO cooling, $13\,M_\odot$ (O yield $0.79\,M_\odot$) fits best. $\gamma$-rays are fully trapped at 200 d, but by 800 d only $\sim20\%$ (th11) to $\sim50\%$ (th21) of the decay power is absorbed; th13 has $\tau_{\rm es}=1.28\rightarrow0.011$ and $L\sim10^{41}\rightarrow10^{38}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$. Dust, not smooth $\gamma$-ray leakage, explains the post-500 d excess fading of $\sim1.5\,\mathrm{mag}$: $0.1\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ silicates with $M_{\rm d}=10^{-4}$, $4\times10^{-3}$, and $5\times10^{-3}\,M_\odot$ at 600, 700, and 800 d, placed at $v<2000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, keep the $V$ offset within $0.2\,\mathrm{mag}$ and are optically thick from the UV through the IR.

analysis.problem: The work asks which progenitor mass is allowed by the nebular spectra of SN 1987A and whether the post-500 d optical deficit and UV behavior come from $\gamma$-ray leakage, molecular cooling, newly formed internal dust, or background-star contamination, rather than from circumstellar interaction.
analysis.method: One-dimensional, time-dependent NLTE radiative transfer with CMFGEN uses shuffled-shell macroscopic mixing and no microscopic mixing. The only power source is radioactive decay, dominated by the $^{56}\mathrm{Ni}$ chain, with nonlocal $\gamma$-ray deposition at gray opacity $\kappa_\gamma=0.06\,Y_e\,\mathrm{cm^{2}\,g^{-1}}$. Molecules are omitted in the global solution; a CO test retains only 10% of the C/O-shell absorbed decay power. After $\sim500\,\mathrm{d}$, $0.1\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ silicate dust is added only inside the metal-rich region at $v<2000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Spectra are placed at $D=49.59\,\mathrm{kpc}$ with $E(B-V)=0.15\,\mathrm{mag}$, and model comparisons are normalized by absorbed decay power.
assumptions: The $^{56}$Ni decay chain dominates the radioactive power at all modeled epochs, and $^{56}$Ni bubbles and CSM interaction are omitted.
limits: Late-time metallicity variations have only a relatively weak spectral effect.

The dashed brown line marks the onset of the higher variability state seen in the 15 and 23.6 GHz light curves, which we use to separate the data into segments 1 and 2 with lower and higher variability, respectively. The shaded region in panels (a), (b), and (c) marks the period MJD 59500–59577 during which simultaneous TESS observations were made. Panel (d) shows the 5-hour binned TESS light curve from sectors 44, 45, and 46. analysis.reason: The paper quantifies when downstream second-order Fermi acceleration at SNR shocks can reshape cosmic-ray spectra and the associated pp gamma-ray flux, which is useful for supernova-shock and high-energy studies, but it does not treat central engines, shock breakout, FRBs, or jets.
analysis.result: Stochastic acceleration appreciably changes the downstream particle spectrum whenever $\eta \gtrsim \xi_{\rm CR}$. For standard Model I parameters, including stochastic acceleration and wave feedback increases the gamma-ray flux between $\sim 1$ and $100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ by $\sim 50\%$. For an undamped $f(p)\propto p^{-4}$ Kolmogorov cascade, $P t_{\rm age}/P_{\rm CR}\approx (3/4)\eta/\xi_{\rm CR}$; acceleration times scale as $\tau_{\rm acc}\sim p^{1/3}$ (Kolmogorov) or $\sim p^{1/2}$ (Kraichnan), while source-free inertial spectra are $W\sim k^{-5/3}$ and $W\sim k^{-3/2}$. Upstream self-generated waves alone do not significantly modify the downstream spectrum because the cascade rapidly removes their energy.
analysis.reading_entry: Evolution of Turbulence and Stochastic Acceleration Downstream
analysis.problem: The paper asks whether particles accelerated at an SNR shock and then advected downstream have their spectrum modified by second-order Fermi acceleration, and whether that change appears in $pp\to\pi^0$ gamma rays, despite strong-shock DSA spectra being nearly universal for $M_s\gg 1$.
analysis.method: The particle distribution and turbulent spectrum are evolved together through $\partial_t f=p^{-2}\partial_p(p^2 D_{pp}\partial_p f)$ and $\partial_t W+\partial_k F=-\Gamma W+S-D$, using quasi-linear $D_{pp}$, resonant damping $\Gamma$, and Kolmogorov or Kraichnan cascades. The SNR downstream is split into independent shells with adiabatic losses, and the $pp$ gamma-ray flux is integrated with Naima and Kafexhiu cross sections, comparing cases with and without stochastic acceleration and wave feedback.
citation_leads: Evolution of Turbulence and Stochastic Acceleration Downstream: “stochastic acceleration to be important whenever $\eta\gtrsim \xi_{\rm CR}$, changing appreciably the particle spectrum.”
Conclusions: “the gamma-ray flux between $\sim 1$ -- 100 GeV increases by $\sim 50\%$ when stochastic acceleration and wave feedback are taken into account.”
analysis.research_progress: Beyond shock-only DSA, the calculation identifies $\eta \gtrsim \xi_{\rm CR}$ as the regime where downstream stochastic acceleration matters and finds a $\sim 50\%$ rise in the $1$--$100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ flux for Model I. Significant modification requires the cascade, wave damping, and a downstream turbulence source to be retained together.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Wave energy spectra (left panel) and accelerated particle spectra (right panel) downstream of a type II SNR, with parameters $\xi_{\rm CR}=0.01$, $\eta=0.1$, $\sigma=0$ and Kraichnan turbulent cascading. Colors indicate fluid parcels that crossed the shock and entered the downstream region at different moments along the SNR’s lifetime, $t_{0}=10$ yr (blue liens), 100 yr (orange lines) and 750 yr (green lines). These spectra evolve from each $t_{0}$ (dashed lines) until the SNR’s age $t_{\rm age}=1000$ yr (solid lines).
figures.label: Fig. 3
figures.physical_core: Downstream of a type II SNR ($\xi_{\rm CR}=0.01$, $\eta=0.1$, $\sigma=0$, Kraichnan cascade), fluid parcels that crossed the shock at $t_0=10$, $100$, and $750$ yr evolve from their injection spectra (dashed) to $t_{\rm age}=1000$ yr (solid). Wave energy $W(k)$ and the particle distribution $f(p)$ change together because resonant damping by the particles is nonlinearly coupled to the turbulence that drives second-order Fermi acceleration.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Hadronic gamma-ray fluxes at $t_{\rm age}=1000$ yr from the downstream of a type II SNR with parameters $\xi_{\rm CR}=0.01$, $\eta=0.1$, $\sigma=0$ and Kraichnan turbulent cascading (same as Figure 3 ), assuming a distance of $d=1$ kpc to us. Fluxes without the effects of stochastic acceleration are shown as dashed lines. The total flux (blue lines) is the sum of the fluxes coming from regions that crossed the shock at all times $t_{0}$ throughout the lifetime of the SNR, which we divide into $0<t_{0}<100$ yr (yellow lines), $100$ yr $<t_{0}<500$ yr (green lines) and $500$ yr $<t_{0}<t_{\rm age}$ (red lines).
figures.label: Fig. 4
figures.physical_core: Hadronic $\gamma$-ray flux at $d=1$ kpc and $t_{\rm age}=1000$ yr from $pp$ scattering in the same downstream. Solid curves include stochastic acceleration; dashed curves do not. The total (blue) is split by shock-crossing epoch: $0<t_0<100$ yr, $100<t_0<500$ yr, and $500\,{\rm yr}<t_0<t_{\rm age}$, so the spectral change is tied to how long each parcel spends in the turbulent downstream.

analysis.reason: The work concerns head-on massive-star collisions, dynamical-friction capture of a stellar-mass black hole, and thermonuclear unbinding, with no substantive link to FRBs, supernova engines, shock breakout, jets, neutrinos, or compact-object high-energy observations.
analysis.result: For $q\le 0.2$, drag dissipation alone does not unbind the star. A star that receives more than half its binding energy during the encounter is destroyed; once the cumulative nuclear release approaches $|E_{\rm bind}|$, the merged system comes apart independent of mass, composition, and drag energy. Here $|E_{\rm bind}|=\tfrac{3}{2}\bar{\beta}\int P\,dV$. In the reported models, burning unbinds the solar-composition $q=0.20$ star ($f_\star=0.16$ versus $0.64$ with nuclear feedback off), while $q=0.10$ leaves a black-hole star.

analysis.reason: The paper is relevant to supernova and compact-merger neutrino transport because collisional flavor conversion need not settle to an attracting fixed point, and the resulting cycles or chaos shift time-averaged flavor populations. It is worth knowing rather than essential because it is a specialized kinetic bifurcation study, not a direct engine or high-energy observational constraint.
analysis.result: Homogeneous collective precession (HCP) is a rotating-frame fixed point, but it is not always attracting. As the electron collision rate $\kappa_e$ approaches $0.0025$ from below, the target growth rate and the HCP number offset vanish together (supercritical Hopf); near $\kappa_e\simeq0.018$ a finite-amplitude pair appears, and the unstable branch merges with the target near $\kappa_e\simeq0.0221$ (subcritical Hopf). An independent HCP crossing occurs at $\kappa_e\simeq0.0200194578$, before target destabilization at $\kappa_e\simeq0.0221481171$. For $0.034\le\kappa_e\le0.060$, successive maxima of $P_z$ period-double eight times toward a stable $256$-cycle, with spacing ratios approaching $\delta_{\rm F}\simeq4.669$. At $\kappa_e=0.055025$ the leading Lyapunov estimate is $\widehat\lambda_1\simeq2.8\times10^{-3}$ for bounded irregular evolution. The HCP balance is $s(u^\star)^2=z^\star\tau^\star$, while averages obey $s[\langle u\rangle_T^2+\mathrm{Var}_T(u)]=\langle z\rangle_T\langle Z\rangle_T+\mathrm{Cov}_T(z,Z)-\tfrac12\mathcal{B}_{u^2}$. The largest reported HCP-versus-time-average population deviation is $8.03\%$, set by the mean coherent torque rather than by stationarity.
analysis.problem: The issue is whether a collisionally balanced HCP state attracts neutrino flavor trajectories or whether collisional flavor instability instead produces Hopf cycles, period doubling, and chaos, and how far HCP or mean-only estimates miss the time-averaged flavor populations.
analysis.method: The full quantum kinetic equations are linearized in the rotating frame, including the response of the self-interaction field; after removal of the common phase, local attraction requires all seven Jacobian eigenvalues to have negative real parts. For energy-independent rates the collective matrix follows the monochromatic kinetics and residuals contract at least as $e^{-\kappa_* t}$. Root number is fixed by the sign of $\mathcal{C}$, and $\kappa_e$ is scanned with multiple shooting and Lyapunov estimates. Steady balance is $s(u^\star)^2=z^\star\tau^\star$, whereas the time-averaged identity keeps $\mathrm{Var}_T(u)$ and $\mathrm{Cov}_T(z,Z)$.
assumptions: Existence of an HCP state does not imply attraction; attraction is judged by linearizing the full quantum kinetic equations in the rotating frame, including self-interaction response.
limits: Because of fluctuation and coherent-torque terms, an HCP estimate need not equal the time average; the maximum reported deviation is $8.03\%$, and relative spectral errors also depend on $c_E$.
citation_leads: Introduction: “Existence does not imply attraction. We linearize the full QKEs in the rotating frame”
Time-averaged populations: “Their difference depends on the mean coherent torque, not on whether the trajectory becomes stationary.”
Time-averaged populations: “where the HCP relation is $s(u^\star)^2=z^\star\tau^\star$. These fluctuation terms explain why an HCP estimate need not equal the time average.”
analysis.research_progress: The advance is a $\kappa_e$ bifurcation sequence for collisional flavor conversion: attracting HCP saturation, supercritical and subcritical Hopf thresholds, a period-doubling cascade with $\delta_{\rm F}\simeq4.669$, and chaos with $\widehat\lambda_1\simeq2.8\times10^{-3}$. When rates are energy independent, spectral residuals decay at least as $e^{-\kappa_* t}$. Time averages share the linear collisional constraint but differ from $s(u^\star)^2=z^\star\tau^\star$ through $\mathrm{Var}_T$, $\mathrm{Cov}_T$, and the mean coherent torque, at the quoted $8.03\%$ level.

analysis.reason: This is a low-latency BNS early-warning search method for third-generation detectors, useful for compact-object multi-messenger follow-up, but it does not directly study FRB/PRS, supernova engines, jets, neutrinos, or circumstellar interaction.
analysis.result: A CNN with $\mathcal{N}=10^{3}$ templates reaches a sensitivity distance comparable to SFT matched filtering, which instead needs approximately $\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{SFT}}=10^{7}$ templates, about four orders of magnitude more. For $f_{\max}=10\,\mathrm{Hz}$ and $f_{\min}\in\{2,3,4,5\}\,\mathrm{Hz}$, the quoted evaluation time falls from minutes to milliseconds, a speed-up of about $1.6\times10^{4}$–$4.0\times10^{4}$; the CNN per-template cost is $\langle\mathfrak{c}_1\rangle\approx(3$–$25)\,\mu\mathrm{s}$. At fixed template number, sensitivity follows $\langle s\rangle\sim\rho_{\rm opt}^{2}(1-\langle\mu\rangle)$ with $\rho_{\rm opt}^{2}\propto\int_{f_{\min}}^{10\,\mathrm{Hz}}f^{-7/3}/S_n(f)\,df$.
analysis.problem: Early warning of binary neutron-star inspirals in third-generation detectors is limited by the computing cost of evaluating the detection statistic at low latency.
analysis.method: Early inspirals are represented by narrowband SFTs with $T_{\mathrm{SFT}}=31\,\mathrm{s}$ and $\Delta k=51$ bins about $f(t;\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}})=f_{\max}[1+(256/5)(\pi f_{\max})^{8/3}(G\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}}/c^{3})^{5/3}(t_{\max}-t)]^{-3/8}$. A CNN minimizes binary cross-entropy and searches only $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{c}}$, while the SFT statistic $\mathcal{X}$ is maximized analytically over phase and luminosity distance and then over an eight-dimensional bank. Latency is modeled as $\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{N}\langle\mathfrak{c}_1\rangle$, with $f_s=40\,\mathrm{Hz}$ for the 3, 4, and 5 Hz regimes.
limits: For lower chirp masses, evolution from $f_{\min}$ to $f_{\max}$ can exceed the fixed analysis window, so the signal is aligned at $f_{\max}$ and only its late portion is retained.

analysis.reason: This ZTF spectroscopic census of hydrogen-rich SLSNe directly constrains circumstellar interaction, pre-explosion mass loss, and possible Ia-CSM contamination, which are central to supernova-engine and CSM studies.
analysis.result: Of 106 hydrogen-rich SLSNe, 105 show narrow Balmer emission and are spectroscopically SLSNe-IIn; SN 2022lvm is the sole broad-lined SLSN-II in the discussed 2021–2022 subset comparison (1/36, 2.8%). Measured $L_{\mathrm{H}\alpha}$ spans $2.2\times10^{40}$ to $1.5\times10^{42}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ (median $2.6\times10^{41}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$). The median Balmer decrement rises from 2.85 before $+100$ d to 4.40 afterward, below the Ia-CSM comparison medians 6.58 and 17.76. After excluding the SLSN-II and six Ia-CSM-like objects, median shell speed correlates with peak magnitude ($r=0.63$, $p=0.010$): brighter events tend to have lower $v_{\rm s}$. For 13 calibrated objects at $v_{\rm CSM}=100\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ and $\epsilon=0.5$, $\dot{M}\sim0.028$–$0.30\,M_{\odot}\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ from $L=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\dot{M}v_{\rm s}^{3}/u_{\rm w}$. Six of 105 narrow-line events ($\sim6\%$) are Ia-CSM-like. Narrow interaction lines can persist beyond $+200$ d, with no Balmer morphology unique to SLSNe-IIn relative to fainter SNe IIn.
analysis.problem: Whether luminous narrow-line SLSNe-IIn are spectroscopically only the bright extreme of SNe IIn, what dense hydrogen-rich CSM and enhanced pre-explosion mass loss they require, and whether narrow Balmer lines plus high luminosity uniquely imply core collapse rather than Ia-CSM.
analysis.method: The study uses 304 optical spectra of 106 ZTF events selected at rest-frame peak $M\leq-19.9$ mag, with phases $(t-t_{\rm peak})/(1+z)$ and fluxes scaled by $10^{-0.4(m_{\rm GP}-m_{\rm syn})}$ from Gaussian-process light curves (287 absolutely calibrated). Balmer luminosity, pEW and FWHM are measured after local continuum subtraction. Single-epoch Monte Carlo electron-scattering snapshots (escatter; $10^{5}$ H$\alpha$ photons outside a cold dense shell) fit line profiles. Mass-loss rates use $L=\frac{1}{2}\epsilon\dot{M}\frac{v_{\rm s}^{3}}{u_{\rm w}}$ and $\dot{M}=\frac{2L}{\epsilon}\frac{u_{\rm w}}{v_{\rm s}^{3}}$, with luminosity integrated from the spectra and a blackbody extension to 3000–20000 Å.
assumptions: Quoted mass-loss rates use the adopted CSM-interaction model with $\epsilon=0.5$ and $v_{\rm CSM}=100\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, commonly with a shock speed of $5000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.
limits: Inferred mass-loss rates are order-of-magnitude estimates rather than precise progenitor mass-loss histories.

analysis.problem: The work asks which progenitor mass is allowed by the nebular spectra of SN 1987A and whether the post-500 d optical deficit and UV behavior come from $\gamma$-ray leakage, molecular cooling, newly formed internal dust, or background-star contamination, rather than from circumstellar interaction.
analysis.method: One-dimensional, time-dependent NLTE radiative transfer with CMFGEN uses shuffled-shell macroscopic mixing and no microscopic mixing. Molecules are omitted in the global solution; a CO test retains only 10% of the C/O-shell absorbed decay power. After $\sim500\,\mathrm{d}$, $0.1\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ silicate dust is added only inside the metal-rich region at $v<2000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Spectra are placed at $D=49.59\,\mathrm{kpc}$ with $E(B-V)=0.15\,\mathrm{mag}$, and model comparisons are normalized by absorbed decay power.
assumptions: The $^{56}$Ni decay chain dominates the radioactive power at all modeled epochs, and $^{56}$Ni bubbles and CSM interaction are omitted.

analysis.reason: This radiative Kerr-magnetosphere GRPIC study is useful for relativistic-jet launching and compact-object VHE emission because it quantifies current closure and gamma-ray output relative to the Blandford–Znajek power, but it is peripheral to FRB, pulsar-wind, and supernova-engine problems.
analysis.result: A polar spark gap and a variable equatorial current sheet jointly sustain the global poloidal current. With low pair multiplicity, synchrotron–curvature (SC) cooling leaves the overall structure largely unchanged but drives spark-gap electric-field oscillations; polar and equatorial variability have no significant cross-correlation and $\Delta t\sim l_{\rm rec}/(\mathcal{R}_{\rm in}c)\sim 10\,r_{\rm g}/c$ at $\mathcal{R}_{\rm in}\sim +0.1$. Post-processed bolometric luminosities are $L_{\rm IC}\sim 10^{-4}L_{\rm BZ}$ and $L_{\rm SC}\sim 10^{-2}L_{\rm BZ}$ (reported in the opening summary as SC up to $\sim 1\%$ and inverse Compton $\sim 0.1\%$ of the BZ luminosity), with spark-gap photons reaching sub-TeV energies. Balancing $t_{\rm SC}=6\pi m_{\rm e}c/(\sigma_{\rm T}f_{\perp,\rm eff}^{2}B_{0}^{2}\Gamma)$ and $t_{\rm acc}\approx\Gamma m_{\rm e}c/(ef_{D}B_{0})$ gives $\Gamma_{\rm max}=\sqrt{f_{D}/f_{\perp,\rm eff}^{2}}\,\Gamma_{\rm SC}\simeq 3.7\times 10^{6}$ for representative equatorial $B_{0}\sim 10^{2}\,\mathrm{G}$.
analysis.problem: The paper investigates how a polar spark gap and an equatorial current sheet jointly close the global poloidal current in a radiative, charge-starved Kerr black-hole magnetosphere, and how SC cooling changes particle acceleration, variability, and gamma-ray signatures relative to observed VHE flares.
analysis.method: The study uses axisymmetric 2D GRPIC in Kerr–Schild 3+1 form, evolving $\frac{1}{c}\partial_t\bm{B}=-\nabla\times\bm{E}$ and $\frac{1}{c}\partial_t\bm{D}=\nabla\times\bm{H}-\frac{4\pi}{c}\bm{J}$ with Hamiltonian particles, ambient-photon inverse Compton scattering, and two-photon pair creation. It compares no cooling, $\Gamma_{\rm SC}=\infty$, with marginal slow cooling, $\Gamma_{\rm SC}=800$, from a Wald vertical field at $a=0.99$, $\tilde{B}_{0}=5\times 10^{3}$, $\varepsilon_{0}=5\times 10^{-2}$, and $\tau_{0}=10$ ($\sigma_{0}\simeq 1.2\times 10^{4}$), followed by ray tracing. The SC drag is $\bm{g}\simeq-\frac{2}{3}\frac{e^{4}}{m_{\rm e}^{2}c^{4}}\Gamma^{2}\bm{\beta}B_{\perp,\rm eff}^{2}$.
assumptions: The adopted plasma supply has a low pair multiplicity, explicitly described as a low-pair-multiplicity parameter choice.
limits: Synthetic luminosity-variation amplitudes are smaller than the order-of-magnitude enhancements in prominent VHE flares.

analysis.research_progress: At low multiplicity, radiative cooling is an incremental correction to force-free current closure: the parabolic near-horizon geometry and global circuit persist, while pair-production efficiency causes gap oscillations. Both regions vary on $\Delta t\lesssim 10\,r_{\rm g}/c$, but only the polar region shows a distinct oscillation peak and their cross-correlation is insignificant. The radiative yields satisfy $L_{\rm SC}\sim 10^{-2}L_{\rm BZ}$ and $L_{\rm IC}\sim 10^{-4}L_{\rm BZ}$, with slow- and fast-cooling spectra $\Gamma dN/d\Gamma\propto\Gamma^{0}$ and $\propto\Gamma^{-1}$.

figures.caption: Figure 7: (a) Time- and volume-averaged particle spectra, $\overline{\Gamma\langle dN/d\Gamma/dV\rangle}$, during $t=219.93\sim 300.26\,r_{\rm g}/c$, for the polar-gap region ($r\leq 3.0\,r_{\rm g}$, $A_{\varphi}\leq A_{\varphi}(r_{\rm h},\pi/4)$). Solid (dashed) curves denote the msCl (nCl) model; blue (orange) curves represent electrons (positrons). (b,c) Temporal evolution of $\Gamma\langle dN/d\Gamma/dV\rangle$ at $\Gamma=\varepsilon_{0}^{-1}$ and the volume-averaged pair-production rate, $\langle\kappa_{\pm}\rangle$. (d–f) Same as (a–c), but for the equatorial current-sheet region ($r\leq 2.0\,r_{\rm g}$, $\theta\leq\pi/2$, $A_{\varphi}\geq A_{\varphi}(r_{\rm h},80^{\circ})$). In panels (a) and (d), green, blue, purple, and red arrows indicate $\Gamma=\varepsilon_{0}^{-1}$, $\Gamma_{\rm cool}$, $\Gamma_{\rm max}(B_{0})=\Gamma_{\rm SC}(f_{D}/f_{B_{\perp,\rm eff}}^{2})^{1/2}$ (Eq. ( 12 ), with $(f_{D},f_{B_{\perp,\rm eff}})=(10^{-1},10^{-1})$ for (a) and $(10^{-1},1.0)$ for (d)), and the time- and volume-averaged magnetization, $\sigma_{\pm}=B^{2}/4\pi n_{\pm}m_{\rm e}c^{2}$, respectively.
figures.label: Fig. 7
figures.physical_core: Time- and volume-averaged particle spectra and the evolution of $\Gamma\langle dN/d\Gamma/dV\rangle$ at $\Gamma=\varepsilon_0^{-1}$ and $\langle\kappa_{\pm}\rangle$ are compared for the polar spark gap and equatorial current sheet, with and without synchrotron-curvature cooling. Markers show $\Gamma_{\rm cool}$, $\Gamma_{\rm max}(B_0)$, and the magnetization $\sigma_{\pm}$; SC cooling truncates and oscillates the gap population, while the sheet spectrum is less sensitive to cooling.

figures.caption: Figure 10: (a) Time-averaged synthetic IC photon spectra during $t_{\rm obs}-r_{\rm obs}/c=220.0\sim 300.0\,r_{\rm g}/c$. (b) Same for SC photons, shown in units of the cyclotron characteristic energy, $\varepsilon_{\rm c}=3heB_{0}/4\pi m_{\rm e}^{2}c^{3}$. Black solid and dash-dotted lines show the total luminosities of the msCl and nCl models. Orange dotted and lime dashed lines indicate contributions from $0<\theta\leq\pi/4$ and $\pi/4<\theta\leq\pi/2$ within $r\sin\theta\leq 3.0\,r_{\rm g}$ for the msCl model.
figures.label: Fig. 10

SC spectra are shown in units of the cyclotron energy $\varepsilon_{\rm c}$, quantifying the high-energy radiative output of both regions.

figures.caption: Figure 7: Synthetic polarization images and quantitative polarization diagnostics produced by the reconnection-bubble model. Rows correspond to cases dominated by radial (top), azimuthal (middle), and vertical (bottom) magnetic perturbations, while all other parameters are kept fixed. From left to right, the columns show representative polarization maps at $t=0$, $5$, and $20$, the azimuthal polarized-intensity variation $\Delta I$, the azimuthal EVPA residual $\Delta{\rm EVPA}$, and the corresponding Stokes- $(Q,U)$ trajectories. The corresponding values of the memory coefficients $(f_{{\rm Mem},r},f_{{\rm Mem},\phi},f_{{\rm Mem},z},f_{{\rm Mem},\chi})$ are indicated in each panel. In all panels, the remaining parameters are fixed at $A_{0}=0.6$, $t_{\rm inj}=1$, $r_{\rm inj}=11$, $\tau_{\rm bubble}=12$, $\tau_{\rm Mem}=20$, and $f_{{\rm Mem},\chi}=0.3$. The observer inclination is fixed at a face-on configuration.
figures.label: Fig. 7
figures.physical_core: With spacetime, emission, and polarization transport fixed, component-dependent reconnection bubbles (mixing $\mathbf{B}=(1-w)\mathbf{B}_{0}+w\mathbf{B}_{\rm bubble}$) yield distinct horizon-scale signatures: radial memory drives inward EVPA shifts, azimuthal memory outward EVPA shifts, and vertical memory mainly suppresses polarized intensity, seen in $\Delta I$, $\Delta{\rm EVPA}$, and Stokes-$(Q,U)$ trajectories at $A_{0}=0.6$, $\tau_{\rm bubble}=12$, $\tau_{\rm Mem}=20$.

analysis.reason: Reports multi-band QPO detections and variability state transition in blazar relativistic jet, providing incremental constraints on jet instabilities and precession models.
analysis.result: Radio QPOs detected at $278\pm3$ days (4.8 GHz, global $2.98\sigma$) and $292\pm6$ days (23.6 GHz, global $3.5\sigma$); optical QPO at $1.4\pm0.1$ days (TESS, global $2.87\sigma$); state transition near MJD 59500 with RMS increase from 0.1 to 0.28 Jy at 23.6 GHz.
analysis.problem: Origin of long-term radio and short-term optical QPOs together with changing variability states in the relativistic jet of BL Lac PKS 0754+100 at $z=0.266$.
analysis.method: Detrended light curves analyzed with GLSP and WWZ; significance via 100000 STINGRAY simulations of broken power-law PSD $P(f)$ under red-noise null hypothesis; trial factor $T=M\times S$ for global significance.
assumptions: The null hypothesis is that the variations in the light curves are only caused by the red noise stochastic variations and no QPO signal is present.

analysis.reason: The paper quantifies when downstream second-order Fermi acceleration at SNR shocks can reshape cosmic-ray spectra and the associated pp gamma-ray flux, which is useful for supernova-shock and high-energy studies, but it does not treat central engines, shock breakout, FRBs, or jets.
analysis.result: Stochastic acceleration appreciably changes the downstream particle spectrum whenever $\eta \gtrsim \xi_{\rm CR}$. For standard Model I parameters, including stochastic acceleration and wave feedback increases the gamma-ray flux between $\sim 1$ and $100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ by $\sim 50\%$. For an undamped $f(p)\propto p^{-4}$ Kolmogorov cascade, $P t_{\rm age}/P_{\rm CR}\approx (3/4)\eta/\xi_{\rm CR}$; acceleration times scale as $\tau_{\rm acc}\sim p^{1/3}$ (Kolmogorov) or $\sim p^{1/2}$ (Kraichnan), while source-free inertial spectra are $W\sim k^{-5/3}$ and $W\sim k^{-3/2}$. Upstream self-generated waves alone do not significantly modify the downstream spectrum because the cascade rapidly removes their energy.
analysis.reading_entry: Evolution of Turbulence and Stochastic Acceleration Downstream
analysis.problem: The paper asks whether particles accelerated at an SNR shock and then advected downstream have their spectrum modified by second-order Fermi acceleration, and whether that change appears in $pp\to\pi^0$ gamma rays, despite strong-shock DSA spectra being nearly universal for $M_s\gg 1$.
analysis.method: The particle distribution and turbulent spectrum are evolved together through $\partial_t f=p^{-2}\partial_p(p^2 D_{pp}\partial_p f)$ and $\partial_t W+\partial_k F=-\Gamma W+S-D$, using quasi-linear $D_{pp}$, resonant damping $\Gamma$, and Kolmogorov or Kraichnan cascades. The SNR downstream is split into independent shells with adiabatic losses, and the $pp$ gamma-ray flux is integrated with Naima and Kafexhiu cross sections, comparing cases with and without stochastic acceleration and wave feedback.
citation_leads: Evolution of Turbulence and Stochastic Acceleration Downstream: “stochastic acceleration to be important whenever $\eta\gtrsim \xi_{\rm CR}$, changing appreciably the particle spectrum.”
Conclusions: “the gamma-ray flux between $\sim 1$ -- 100 GeV increases by $\sim 50\%$ when stochastic acceleration and wave feedback are taken into account.”
analysis.research_progress: Beyond shock-only DSA, the calculation identifies $\eta \gtrsim \xi_{\rm CR}$ as the regime where downstream stochastic acceleration matters and finds a $\sim 50\%$ rise in the $1$--$100\,\mathrm{GeV}$ flux for Model I. Significant modification requires the cascade, wave damping, and a downstream turbulence source to be retained together.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Wave energy spectra (left panel) and accelerated particle spectra (right panel) downstream of a type II SNR, with parameters $\xi_{\rm CR}=0.01$, $\eta=0.1$, $\sigma=0$ and Kraichnan turbulent cascading. Colors indicate fluid parcels that crossed the shock and entered the downstream region at different moments along the SNR’s lifetime, $t_{0}=10$ yr (blue liens), 100 yr (orange lines) and 750 yr (green lines). These spectra evolve from each $t_{0}$ (dashed lines) until the SNR’s age $t_{\rm age}=1000$ yr (solid lines).
figures.label: Fig. 3
figures.physical_core: Downstream of a type II SNR ($\xi_{\rm CR}=0.01$, $\eta=0.1$, $\sigma=0$, Kraichnan cascade), fluid parcels that crossed the shock at $t_0=10$, $100$, and $750$ yr evolve from their injection spectra (dashed) to $t_{\rm age}=1000$ yr (solid). Wave energy $W(k)$ and the particle distribution $f(p)$ change together because resonant damping by the particles is nonlinearly coupled to the turbulence that drives second-order Fermi acceleration.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Hadronic gamma-ray fluxes at $t_{\rm age}=1000$ yr from the downstream of a type II SNR with parameters $\xi_{\rm CR}=0.01$, $\eta=0.1$, $\sigma=0$ and Kraichnan turbulent cascading (same as Figure 3 ), assuming a distance of $d=1$ kpc to us. Fluxes without the effects of stochastic acceleration are shown as dashed lines. The total flux (blue lines) is the sum of the fluxes coming from regions that crossed the shock at all times $t_{0}$ throughout the lifetime of the SNR, which we divide into $0<t_{0}<100$ yr (yellow lines), $100$ yr $<t_{0}<500$ yr (green lines) and $500$ yr $<t_{0}<t_{\rm age}$ (red lines).
figures.label: Fig. 4
figures.physical_core: Hadronic $\gamma$-ray flux at $d=1$ kpc and $t_{\rm age}=1000$ yr from $pp$ scattering in the same downstream. Solid curves include stochastic acceleration; dashed curves do not. The total (blue) is split by shock-crossing epoch: $0<t_0<100$ yr, $100<t_0<500$ yr, and $500\,{\rm yr}<t_0<t_{\rm age}$, so the spectral change is tied to how long each parcel spends in the turbulent downstream.

analysis.result: Homogeneous collective precession (HCP) is a rotating-frame fixed point, but it is not always attracting. As the electron collision rate $\kappa_e$ approaches $0.0025$ from below, the target growth rate and the HCP number offset vanish together (supercritical Hopf); near $\kappa_e\simeq0.018$ a finite-amplitude pair appears, and the unstable branch merges with the target near $\kappa_e\simeq0.0221$ (subcritical Hopf). An independent HCP crossing occurs at $\kappa_e\simeq0.0200194578$, before target destabilization at $\kappa_e\simeq0.0221481171$. analysis.reason: The paper establishes an intrinsic hard X-ray point-source excess in the Nuclear Stellar Disk and associates it with high-mass white-dwarf intermediate polars and possibly millisecond pulsars, which is relevant compact-object high-energy context but not central to FRB, jet, neutrino, or supernova-engine studies.
analysis.result: Within the NSD ($|l|\lesssim 1.3^{\circ}$, $|b|\lesssim 0.3^{\circ}$), XMM-Newton finds a concentration of intrinsically hard point sources. Plane sources are softer, with mean $\mathrm{HR}\simeq 0.1$ (PN) and $\simeq-0.3$ (MOS), where $\mathrm{HR}\equiv(H-S)/(H+S)$, $H=4.5$–$12\,\mathrm{keV}$, and $S=2.0$–$4.5\,\mathrm{keV}$. Inside-versus-outside HR distributions differ at $>8\sigma$. At $-1.05^{\circ}<l<0.55^{\circ}$, observed $\mathrm{HR}\gtrsim 0.3$ exceeds $\mathrm{HR}<0.2$ predicted for $5\times10^{22}<N_{\rm H}<8\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$. Hard and soft longitude/latitude distributions differ at $>12\sigma/9\sigma$ ($p=2\times10^{-35}/3\times10^{-20}$). Scale heights are $h_{l,\rm s}=2^{\circ}$ ($\sim280\,\mathrm{pc}$), $h_{b,\rm s}=0.31^{\circ}$ ($\sim44\,\mathrm{pc}$), $h_{l,\rm h}=0.66^{\circ}$ ($\sim90\,\mathrm{pc}$), and $h_{b,\rm h}=0.17^{\circ}$ ($\sim24\,\mathrm{pc}$). The stellar-mass distribution follows the soft sources better than the hard sources. The hard NSD population most likely consists of intermediate polars with high $M_{\rm WD}$, possibly plus MSPs; representative partial covering at $kT=36\,\mathrm{keV}$ gives $\mathrm{HR}\sim0.82$ versus $\sim0.36$ without it, and $\langle kT\rangle\approx34\,\mathrm{keV}$ for IPs versus $\approx11\,\mathrm{keV}$ for polars. The $\log N$–$\log S$ slope is $\alpha\sim1.35$–$1.5$.
analysis.problem: The paper tests whether the hard X-ray point-source concentration overlapping the NSD is an intrinsically harder compact-object population or only an artifact of large line-of-sight $N_{\rm H}$, and what that population implies for the unresolved sources underlying the Galactic-center and Galactic-ridge X-ray emission.
analysis.method: Using the XMM-Newton Heritage Survey and cleaned 4XMM-DR14 sources over $|l|<10^{\circ}$, $|b|<1^{\circ}$, the authors compare $\mathrm{HR}\equiv(H-S)/(H+S)$ inside and outside the NSD with count-rate and exposure-matched K–S tests. Because most sources lack reliable spectra, they simulate 274 parameter sets with XSPEC fakeit and EPIC-PN responses: $\mathrm{tbabs}\times\mathrm{powerlaw}$ for $\Gamma=0$–$3$ and absorbed APEC for $kT=1$–$36\,\mathrm{keV}$, spanning $N_{\rm H}=(1$–$30)\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ and $Z_{\rm Fe}=(0.5,1,2)Z_{\odot}$.

analysis.result: IXPE measures a 2–8 keV polarization of $(4.01\pm 0.20)\%$ parallel to the radio jet at inclination $27.51^\circ$, whereas static corona models give only $1$–$2.5\%$. Cylindrical outflow models with $h=H/(2R)\leq 0.8$ and $\beta_{\rm top}=0.5$–$0.9$ simultaneously give $\Gamma=1.6$ and $\sim 4\%$ polarization parallel to the symmetry axis; larger $h$ has $q_{\rm max}<4\%$ even at $\beta_{\rm top}=0.99$. Outflow suppresses radiative feedback as $f_\beta\propto(1-\beta)^2$. The discussion gives $\delta\approx 1.56$, $L\approx 0.3L_{\rm iso}$, $\ell=35.4(L_{\rm iso}/0.5\%L_{\rm Edd})(r_g/R)$, $t_{\rm IC}=0.03(R/r_g)R/c$, $B_{\rm eq}\approx 1.1\times 10^{7}(R/r_g)^{-1}\,\mathrm{G}$, $\sigma\approx 6.9(R/r_g)^{-1}$ and $v_A\approx 0.9c$, favoring a pair corona. The IXPE polarization-angle difference is $3.3^\circ\pm 3.2^\circ$; requiring the band-to-band Faraday difference to be $<0.11$ rad yields $\eta_\Delta<0.14(B_\parallel/10^{7}\,\mathrm{G})^{-1}$.
